cards.title: State the **Riemann sum** of $f$ on $[a, b]$ with $n$ equal subintervals and sample points $x_i^*$.
cards.body:
$\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$, where $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i^*$ is a point chosen in the $i$-th subinterval $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

Cutting $[a, b]$ at the points $a = x_0 < x_1 < \dots < x_n = b$ is called a **partition**; with equal widths, $x_i = a + i\,\Delta x$. Each term $f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$ is the area of a thin rectangle of height $f(x_i^*)$ and width $\Delta x$.

Why: Adding up thin rectangles approximates the area under a curve, and thinner rectangles should approximate it better.

Watch out: The sample point may be the left end, the right end or the midpoint of each subinterval. The three choices give different sums for the same $n$.

cards.title: Define the **definite integral** $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ as a limit of Riemann sums.
cards.body:
$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$ with $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$, when the limit exists and is the same for every choice of sample points $x_i^*$; $f$ is the **integrand**.

Every continuous function on $[a, b]$ has this limit, so continuous functions can always be integrated.

Example: For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ with right endpoints, $R_n = \frac{1}{n^3}\sum_{i=1}^n i^2 = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6n^2}$, which tends to $\frac13$. So $\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac13$.

Key idea: The integral is defined by a limit, not by antiderivatives. The link between the two is the fundamental theorem, coming next.

cards.title: How does $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ count area when $f$ is negative on part of $[a, b]$?
cards.body:
As **net signed area**: area between the graph and the $x$-axis counts as positive where $f > 0$ and as negative where $f < 0$.

Why: Where $f(x_i^*) < 0$, the rectangle in a Riemann sum has negative height, so its term is negative, and that survives in the limit.

Example: $\int_0^4 (x-2)\,dx$. The graph is a line through $(2, 0)$. Between $0$ and $2$ it bounds a triangle of area $\frac12\cdot 2\cdot 2 = 2$ below the axis, and between $2$ and $4$ a triangle of the same area above it. The integral is $-2 + 2 = 0$.

Watch out: A definite integral of $0$ does not mean there is no area, only that the positive and negative parts cancel.

cards.title: Write the right-endpoint sum $R_n$ of $f$ on $[a, b]$ using $a$ and $\Delta x$, and say which indices give the left-endpoint sum $L_n$.
cards.body:
$R_n = \Delta x\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(a + i\,\Delta x)$ with $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$; the left-endpoint sum $L_n$ uses $f(a + (i-1)\Delta x)$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$.

The midpoint sum $M_n$ uses $f\big(a + (i - \tfrac12)\Delta x\big)$.

Why: The $i$-th subinterval is $[a + (i-1)\Delta x,\ a + i\,\Delta x]$, so its right end is $a + i\,\Delta x$.

Key idea: $L_n$ and $R_n$ share all their terms except one at each end, so $R_n - L_n = \Delta x\,\big(f(b) - f(a)\big)$. If $f$ is increasing, $L_n \le \int_a^b f \le R_n$; if decreasing, the inequalities reverse.

cards.title: State the **comparison property** of the definite integral.
cards.body:
If $f$ and $g$ are integrable on $[a, b]$ with $a < b$ and $f(x) \le g(x)$ for all $x \in [a, b]$, then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx \le \int_a^b g(x)\,dx$.

In particular, if $m \le f(x) \le M$ on $[a, b]$, then $m(b-a) \le \int_a^b f(x)\,dx \le M(b-a)$.

Why: With the same sample points, every Riemann sum of $f$ is at most the matching sum of $g$, and limits preserve $\le$.

Example: On $[0, 1]$ we have $1 \le e^{x^2} \le e$, so $1 \le \int_0^1 e^{x^2}\,dx \le e$, with no antiderivative needed.

Watch out: The condition $a < b$ matters. The inequality is about the order of the functions, not of the limits.

cards.title: Estimate $\int_0^2 x^2\,dx$ by the midpoint sum $M_4$ ($n = 4$ equal subintervals). Give the number.
cards.body:
$M_4 = 2.625$

Here $\Delta x = \frac{2-0}{4} = 0.5$, so the midpoints are $0.25,\ 0.75,\ 1.25,\ 1.75$.

1. Heights: $0.0625,\ 0.5625,\ 1.5625,\ 3.0625$.
2. Their sum is $5.25$.
3. Multiply by $\Delta x$: $M_4 = 0.5 \times 5.25 = 2.625$.

Check: The exact value is $\frac83 \approx 2.667$. For comparison, $L_4 = 1.75$ and $R_4 = 3.75$ are far off, because $x^2$ is increasing and they miss on opposite sides. The midpoint sum is usually much closer.

cards.title: Suppose $\int_0^3 f(x)\,dx = 4$ and $\int_3^7 f(x)\,dx = 5$. Find $\int_0^7 \big(2f(x) - 1\big)\,dx$.
cards.body:
$11$

Two properties do the work, both valid when the integrals exist:

- Additivity over intervals: $\int_a^c f = \int_a^b f + \int_b^c f$ for $a < b < c$.
- Linearity: $\int_a^b (c\,f + g) = c\int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$.

1. Additivity: $\int_0^7 f = 4 + 5 = 9$.
2. Linearity: $\int_0^7 (2f - 1) = 2\cdot 9 - \int_0^7 1\,dx$.
3. The constant $1$ on $[0, 7]$ is a rectangle of height $1$ and width $7$, so $\int_0^7 1\,dx = 7$.
4. Result: $18 - 7 = 11$.

Watch out: The constant $-1$ contributes $-1\cdot(b-a)$, not just $-1$.

cards.title: Why is “$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is a function of $x$” false?
cards.body:
The definite integral is a single number that depends on $f$, $a$ and $b$; $x$ is a dummy variable that can be renamed, so $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(t)\,dt$.

Why: The Riemann sum in the definition adds up over $i$ and takes a limit in $n$. No $x$ is left once the limit is taken, just as no $i$ is left in $\sum_{i=1}^n i$.

Example: $\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac13$ is just the number $\frac13$. It has no $x$ in it.

Watch out: This is the difference from an indefinite integral $\int f(x)\,dx$, which is a family of functions. Putting a variable in a limit, as in $\int_a^x f(t)\,dt$, does give a function of $x$, and that is the topic of the next unit.

cards.title: What is an **accumulation function**, and why is it written $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ with a $t$ inside?
cards.body:
It gives the net signed area of $f$ from the fixed point $a$ up to a moving point $x$, so it is a function of $x$; the inner variable $t$ is a dummy so that it does not clash with the upper limit $x$.

Example: For $f(t) = t$ and $a = 0$, the region from $0$ to $x$ is a triangle with base $x$ and height $x$, so $F(x) = \frac{x^2}{2}$. For the constant $f(t) = 2$, $F(x) = 2x$.

Key idea: In both examples $F'(x) = f(x)$. The fundamental theorem says this is no accident.

Watch out: $\int_a^x f(x)\,dx$ is a bad way to write this, because $x$ would be both the limit and the variable being summed.

cards.title: State **part 1 of the fundamental theorem of calculus**.
cards.body:
If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt$ for $x \in [a, b]$, then $F$ is continuous on $[a, b]$, differentiable on $(a, b)$, and $F'(x) = f(x)$.

Key idea of the proof: $F(x+h) - F(x) = \int_x^{x+h} f(t)\,dt$ lies between $h$ times the smallest and $h$ times the largest value of $f$ on that short interval. Divide by $h$ and let $h \to 0$: by continuity both bounds tend to $f(x)$.

Why it matters: Every continuous function has an antiderivative, namely its accumulation function, even when no formula for it exists.

Watch out: Continuity of $f$ is what makes $F' = f$ hold at every $x$.

cards.title: State **part 2 of the fundamental theorem of calculus** (the evaluation theorem).
cards.body:
If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $F$ is any antiderivative of $f$ on $[a, b]$ (that is, $F' = f$), then $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$.

The right side is often written $\big[F(x)\big]_a^b$.

Why: The accumulation function $G(x) = \int_a^x f$ is also an antiderivative of $f$ by part 1. Two antiderivatives differ by a constant, so $F = G + C$, and $F(b) - F(a) = G(b) - G(a) = \int_a^b f - 0$.

Example: $\int_0^2 x^2\,dx = \big[\frac{x^3}{3}\big]_0^2 = \frac83$, a value Riemann sums only approach in the limit.

Tip: Any antiderivative works. The constant $C$ cancels in $F(b) - F(a)$.

cards.title: Give the formula for the **average value** of a continuous function $f$ on $[a, b]$.
cards.body:
$f_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{1}{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$

Why: Take $n$ sample values and average them: $\frac1n\sum f(x_i^*)$. Since $\frac1n = \frac{\Delta x}{b-a}$, this equals $\frac{1}{b-a}\sum f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x$, which tends to the formula above.

Example: For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 3]$, $\int_0^3 x^2\,dx = 9$, so $f_{\text{avg}} = \frac93 = 3$. The function takes the value $3$ at $x = \sqrt3$ inside the interval.

Key idea: A continuous function actually reaches its average value somewhere on $[a, b]$, so the rectangle of height $f_{\text{avg}}$ has the same area as the region under the graph.

cards.title: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_1^{x^2} e^{t^2}\,dt$.
cards.body:
$2x\,e^{x^4}$

Name the accumulation function $A(u) = \int_1^u e^{t^2}\,dt$. Part 1 gives $A'(u) = e^{u^2}$. The expression in question is $A(x^2)$, so the chain rule applies.

In general, for $f$ continuous and $g$ differentiable: $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^{g(x)} f(t)\,dt = f(g(x))\,g'(x)$.

1. Evaluate the integrand at the upper limit: $e^{(x^2)^2} = e^{x^4}$.
2. Multiply by the derivative of the limit: $\frac{d}{dx}x^2 = 2x$.

Watch out: Forgetting the factor $g'(x)$ is the usual slip. Also, the integral itself is never computed, since $e^{t^2}$ has no elementary antiderivative.

cards.title: Use the **net change theorem** for a particle with velocity $v(t) = 2t - 4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ on $0 \le t \le 5$. Find the displacement and the total distance traveled.
cards.body:
Displacement $5\ \mathrm{m}$; total distance $13\ \mathrm{m}$.

The net change theorem: if $F'$ is continuous, then $\int_a^b F'(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$. The integral of a rate of change is the net change. It is part 2 of the fundamental theorem with a new reading.

1. Displacement $= \int_0^5 (2t-4)\,dt = \big[t^2 - 4t\big]_0^5 = 25 - 20 = 5$.
2. The velocity is negative for $t < 2$ and positive for $t > 2$, so distance needs $|v|$ and a split at $t = 2$.
3. $\int_0^2 |v| = -\big[t^2 - 4t\big]_0^2 = -(4 - 8) = 4$.
4. $\int_2^5 |v| = \big[t^2 - 4t\big]_2^5 = 5 - (-4) = 9$.
5. Distance $= 4 + 9 = 13$.

Watch out: Displacement uses $v$, distance uses $|v|$. They differ whenever the particle turns around.

cards.title: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\displaystyle\int_x^{x^2}\sqrt{1+t^4}\,dt$ for $x > 0$.
cards.body:
$2x\sqrt{1+x^8} - \sqrt{1+x^4}$

Neither limit is constant, so split at a fixed point such as $0$. With the convention $\int_b^a f = -\int_a^b f$, additivity gives $\int_x^{x^2} = \int_0^{x^2} - \int_0^{x}$.

1. Differentiate the first piece using the chain rule version of part 1: $\sqrt{1 + (x^2)^4}\cdot 2x = 2x\sqrt{1+x^8}$.
2. Differentiate the second piece: $\sqrt{1+x^4}$.
3. Subtract: $2x\sqrt{1+x^8} - \sqrt{1+x^4}$.

Tip: A moving lower limit contributes with a minus sign, because swapping the limits flips the sign of the integral.

cards.title: Why is $\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = \Big[-\frac1x\Big]_{-1}^{1} = -2$ wrong?
cards.body:
Part 2 of the fundamental theorem needs $f$ continuous on the whole interval, and $\frac{1}{x^2}$ is unbounded near $x = 0$, so the calculation does not apply.

A quick sanity check shows the answer cannot be right: the integrand is positive everywhere, so any integral of it must be positive, not $-2$.

Why: The antiderivative $-\frac1x$ blows up at $0$. It is not an antiderivative on $[-1, 1]$, so $F(1) - F(-1)$ says nothing about the area. The area on each side of $0$ grows without bound.

Tip: Before applying $F(b) - F(a)$, check that the integrand is continuous on the closed interval. A negative answer for a positive function is a red flag.

cards.title: What does the **substitution rule** do, and which rule of differentiation does it reverse?
cards.body:
It reverses the chain rule: $\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du$ with $u = g(x)$, valid for $g'$ continuous and $f$ continuous on the range of $g$.

Why: By the chain rule, $\frac{d}{dx}F(g(x)) = F'(g(x))\,g'(x) = f(g(x))\,g'(x)$ when $F' = f$. So $F(g(x))$ is an antiderivative of the left-hand integrand.

Tip: Look for an inner function whose derivative (up to a constant factor) also appears in the integrand. In $\int 2x\cos(x^2)\,dx$, take $u = x^2$, so $du = 2x\,dx$ and the result is $\sin(x^2) + C$.

Watch out: After substituting, no $x$ may remain. If one does, the choice of $u$ was wrong or more algebra is needed.

cards.title: State the substitution rule for **definite integrals**.
cards.body:
$\int_a^b f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)\,du$, for $g'$ continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f$ continuous on the range of $g$.

Why: If $F' = f$, both sides equal $F(g(b)) - F(g(a))$ by part 2 of the fundamental theorem.

Key idea: Convert the limits along with the variable and the integrand, and then there is no need to return to $x$.

Watch out: The new limits are $g(a)$ and $g(b)$, in that order. The lower new limit may be larger than the upper one, which is fine.

cards.title: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^2 \frac{e^{1/x}}{x^2}\,dx$ by substitution.
cards.body:
$e - \sqrt{e}$

1. Let $u = \frac1x$, so $du = -\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$, that is, $\frac{dx}{x^2} = -du$.
2. Limits: $x = 1$ gives $u = 1$, and $x = 2$ gives $u = \frac12$.
3. The integral becomes $\int_1^{1/2} -e^u\,du = \int_{1/2}^{1} e^u\,du$, flipping the limits to remove the minus sign.
4. $= e^1 - e^{1/2} = e - \sqrt e$.

Check: The integrand is positive on $[1, 2]$ and the result $\approx 1.07$ is positive. 

Watch out: Here the substitution makes the limits run downward, from $1$ to $\frac12$. That is allowed, and the minus sign from $du$ accounts for it.

cards.title: State the formula for **integration by parts**, in indefinite and definite form.
cards.body:
$\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du$, and $\int_a^b f(x)\,g'(x)\,dx = \big[f(x)\,g(x)\big]_a^b - \int_a^b f'(x)\,g(x)\,dx$.

Why: It is the product rule integrated. From $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$ we get $\int fg' = fg - \int f'g$, with $u = f$ and $dv = g'\,dx$.

Key idea: The method pays off when $\int v\,du$ is simpler than $\int u\,dv$: $u$ should get simpler on differentiating, and $dv$ should be easy to integrate.

Watch out: In the definite form, the boundary term $[fg]_a^b$ is evaluated at both limits.

cards.title: Use the **LIATE heuristic** to choose $u$ and evaluate $\int x\log x\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\frac{x^2}{2}\log x - \frac{x^2}{4} + C$

LIATE ranks the candidates for $u$: Logarithmic, Inverse trigonometric, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. Pick $u$ from the earliest type present. It is a rule of thumb, not a theorem.

1. Here $\log x$ comes before the algebraic $x$, so $u = \log x$ and $dv = x\,dx$.
2. Then $du = \frac1x\,dx$ and $v = \frac{x^2}{2}$.
3. $\int x\log x\,dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\log x - \int \frac{x^2}{2}\cdot\frac1x\,dx = \frac{x^2}{2}\log x - \frac{x^2}{4} + C$.

Check: Differentiating gives $x\log x + \frac x2 - \frac x2 = x\log x$.

Watch out: The reverse choice $u = x$ would need an antiderivative of $\log x$ first, which is harder.

cards.title: Evaluate $\int x^2 e^x\,dx$, and write the **reduction formula** for $\int x^n e^x\,dx$ that your steps follow.
cards.body:
$e^x\,(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C$; the reduction formula is $\int x^n e^x\,dx = x^n e^x - n\int x^{n-1} e^x\,dx$.

A **reduction formula** expresses an integral in terms of a similar one with a smaller parameter, so applying it repeatedly finishes the job.

1. Parts with $u = x^2$, $dv = e^x\,dx$: $\int x^2 e^x\,dx = x^2 e^x - 2\int x e^x\,dx$.
2. Parts again with $u = x$: $\int x e^x\,dx = x e^x - \int e^x\,dx = x e^x - e^x$.
3. Combine: $x^2 e^x - 2x e^x + 2e^x + C = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C$.

Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\big[e^x(x^2-2x+2)\big] = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2 + 2x - 2) = x^2 e^x$.

cards.title: Evaluate $\int e^x\sin x\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\frac{e^x}{2}(\sin x - \cos x) + C$

Neither factor gets simpler under differentiation, so by parts twice returns the original integral, which can then be solved for.

1. Let $I = \int e^x\sin x\,dx$. With $u = \sin x$, $dv = e^x\,dx$: $I = e^x\sin x - \int e^x\cos x\,dx$.
2. By parts again, $u = \cos x$, $dv = e^x\,dx$: $\int e^x\cos x\,dx = e^x\cos x + \int e^x\sin x\,dx = e^x\cos x + I$.
3. So $I = e^x\sin x - e^x\cos x - I$, hence $2I = e^x(\sin x - \cos x)$.
4. Divide by $2$ and add the constant.

Watch out: Use the same type of choice for $u$ in both rounds (trigonometric for $u$ each time). Switching in the second round undoes the first and gives $0 = 0$.

cards.title: Evaluate $\int_0^1 \arctan x\,dx$, using $\frac{d}{dx}\arctan x = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$.
cards.body:
$\frac{\pi}{4} - \frac12\log 2$

Write the integrand as $\arctan x\cdot 1$ and use parts, taking $u = \arctan x$ (an inverse trigonometric function, which LIATE puts first) and $dv = dx$.

1. $du = \frac{dx}{1+x^2}$ and $v = x$.
2. $\int_0^1 \arctan x\,dx = \big[x\arctan x\big]_0^1 - \int_0^1\frac{x}{1+x^2}\,dx$.
3. The boundary term is $1\cdot\frac\pi4 - 0 = \frac\pi4$.
4. For the last integral let $w = 1 + x^2$, $dw = 2x\,dx$, limits $1$ to $2$: $\frac12\int_1^2\frac{dw}{w} = \frac12\log 2$.
5. Result: $\frac\pi4 - \frac12\log 2 \approx 0.439$.

Tip: When the integrand is a single function with no obvious product, such as $\log x$ or $\arctan x$, try $dv = dx$.

cards.title: Why is it wrong to evaluate $\int_1^2 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx$ as $\int_1^2 e^u\,du$ after setting $u = x^2$?
cards.body:
The limits $1$ and $2$ are values of $x$; after substituting they must become the values of $u$, namely $u = 1$ and $u = 4$, so the correct result is $\int_1^4 e^u\,du = e^4 - e$.

The wrong version gives $e^2 - e$.

Why: The definite-integral rule integrates from $g(a)$ to $g(b)$. A limit written next to $du$ is a value of $u$, not of $x$.

Tip: Either change the limits as you substitute, or find the antiderivative in $u$, convert back to $x$, and use the original limits. Never mix the two.

Watch out: The slip is easy to miss when $g(a) = a$ and $g(b) = b$, as with $u = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$, where the wrong method happens to work.

cards.title: What is a **partial fraction decomposition**, and which terms does each kind of factor of the denominator produce?
cards.body:
It rewrites a rational function $\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$, with $\deg P < \deg Q$, as a sum of simpler fractions: a factor $(x - r)^k$ in $Q$ gives $\frac{A_1}{x-r} + \dots + \frac{A_k}{(x-r)^k}$, and an **irreducible quadratic factor** $(x^2 + bx + c)^k$, one with no real roots, gives $\frac{B_1x + C_1}{x^2+bx+c} + \dots + \frac{B_kx + C_k}{(x^2+bx+c)^k}$.

Why: Each simple piece integrates easily: $\frac{A}{x-r}$ to a logarithm, and $\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+bx+c}$ to a logarithm plus an arctangent.

Example: $\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{1/3}{x-1} - \frac{1/3}{x+2}$.

Tip: Find the constants by clearing denominators, then either plugging in convenient values of $x$ or matching coefficients of like powers.

cards.title: Give the **trigonometric substitution** for each of $\sqrt{a^2 - x^2}$, $\sqrt{a^2 + x^2}$ and $\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$ (with $a > 0$).
cards.body:
$\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$: $x = a\sin\theta$; $\sqrt{a^2+x^2}$: $x = a\tan\theta$; $\sqrt{x^2-a^2}$: $x = a\sec\theta$, where $\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}$ is the **secant**.

Why: Each choice turns the root into a single trigonometric function through a Pythagorean identity: $a^2 - a^2\sin^2\theta = a^2\cos^2\theta$, $a^2 + a^2\tan^2\theta = a^2\sec^2\theta$, $a^2\sec^2\theta - a^2 = a^2\tan^2\theta$.

Key idea: Take $\theta \in [-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2]$ for the sine substitution, $\theta \in (-\frac\pi2, \frac\pi2)$ for tangent, and $\theta \in [0, \frac\pi2) \cup [\pi, \frac{3\pi}{2})$ for secant. On these ranges $\cos\theta$, $\sec\theta$ and $\tan\theta$ have the sign that makes each root equal $a\cos\theta$, $a\sec\theta$ and $a\tan\theta$ exactly, with no absolute values.

Tip: Draw a right triangle to convert the final answer from $\theta$ back to $x$.

cards.title: State $\int\sec x\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\log|\sec x + \tan x| + C$

Why: Differentiate: $\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x + \tan x) = \sec x\tan x + \sec^2 x = \sec x(\tan x + \sec x)$. Dividing by $\sec x + \tan x$ leaves $\sec x$, so the chain rule for $\log$ gives the result.

Why it matters: It is the key step in several **trigonometric integrals**, such as $\int\sec^3 x\,dx$, and in trig substitutions with $x = a\tan\theta$.

Tip: The proof is a trick. Memorize the result, rather than expecting to find it by technique.

cards.title: Evaluate $\int\sin^3 x\cos^2 x\,dx$.
cards.body:
$-\frac{\cos^3 x}{3} + \frac{\cos^5 x}{5} + C$

When the power of sine is odd, split off one $\sin x$ and rewrite the rest using $\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$. The leftover $\sin x\,dx$ is $-du$ for $u = \cos x$.

1. $\sin^3 x\cos^2 x = (1 - \cos^2 x)\cos^2 x\,\sin x$.
2. With $u = \cos x$, $du = -\sin x\,dx$: $-\int (1 - u^2)\,u^2\,du = -\int (u^2 - u^4)\,du$.
3. $= -\frac{u^3}{3} + \frac{u^5}{5} + C$.

Tip: If the cosine power is odd, do the same with the roles swapped ($u = \sin x$). If both powers are even, use the half-angle formulas to lower the powers.

cards.title: Evaluate $\int\frac{dx}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+4}}$ by trigonometric substitution.
cards.body:
$-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{4x} + C$

The form $\sqrt{x^2 + 4}$ suggests $x = 2\tan\theta$.

1. Then $dx = 2\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{x^2+4} = 2\sec\theta$, taking $-\frac\pi2<\theta<\frac\pi2$.
2. The integral becomes $\int\frac{2\sec^2\theta}{4\tan^2\theta\cdot 2\sec\theta}\,d\theta = \frac14\int\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan^2\theta}\,d\theta = \frac14\int\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin^2\theta}\,d\theta$.
3. With $w = \sin\theta$: $\frac14\int w^{-2}\,dw = -\frac{1}{4\sin\theta} + C$.
4. From the triangle with legs $x$ and $2$ and hypotenuse $\sqrt{x^2+4}$, $\sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+4}}$.
5. So the answer is $-\frac{\sqrt{x^2+4}}{4x} + C$.

Check: Differentiating gives $\frac{1}{x^2\sqrt{x^2+4}}$.

cards.title: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+1)}\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\frac32\log|x-1| - \frac14\log(x^2+1) - \frac12\arctan x + C$

1. Set up: $\frac{x^2+2}{(x-1)(x^2+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}$, so $x^2 + 2 = A(x^2+1) + (Bx+C)(x-1)$.
2. Put $x = 1$: $3 = 2A$, so $A = \frac32$.
3. Compare $x^2$ coefficients: $1 = A + B$, so $B = -\frac12$. Compare constants: $2 = A - C$, so $C = -\frac12$.
4. Integrate: $\frac32\int\frac{dx}{x-1} - \frac12\int\frac{x}{x^2+1}\,dx - \frac12\int\frac{dx}{x^2+1}$.
5. The middle integral is $\frac12\cdot\frac12\log(x^2+1)$ by $w = x^2+1$, and the last is $\arctan x$.

Check: The $x$ coefficients on both sides: $0 = -B + C = \frac12 - \frac12$, as required.
cards.searchQuery: partial fractions integral (x^2+2)/((x-1)(x^2+1)) arctan

cards.title: Evaluate $\int\sin^2 x\cos^2 x\,dx$.
cards.body:
$\frac{x}{8} - \frac{\sin 4x}{32} + C$

Both powers are even, so no substitution works directly. Use the double-angle formula to lower the powers.

1. $\sin x\cos x = \frac12\sin 2x$, so $\sin^2 x\cos^2 x = \frac14\sin^2 2x$.
2. Half-angle formula: $\sin^2 2x = \frac{1 - \cos 4x}{2}$, so the integrand is $\frac{1 - \cos 4x}{8}$.
3. $\int\frac{1-\cos 4x}{8}\,dx = \frac x8 - \frac{\sin 4x}{32} + C$.

Tip: For even powers, repeated half-angle reductions ($\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}$, $\cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}$) turn the integrand into a sum of cosines that integrate directly.
cards.searchQuery: integral sin^2 x cos^2 x even powers double angle formula

cards.title: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{1-x^2}\,dx$ by trigonometric substitution, and say what it measures.
cards.body:
$\frac\pi4$, the area of a quarter of the unit disk.

1. The root $\sqrt{1 - x^2}$ suggests $x = \sin\theta$, so $dx = \cos\theta\,d\theta$ and $\sqrt{1-x^2} = \cos\theta$ for $0\le\theta\le\frac\pi2$.
2. The limits change: $x = 0$ gives $\theta = 0$ and $x = 1$ gives $\theta = \frac\pi2$.
3. The integral becomes $\int_0^{\pi/2}\cos^2\theta\,d\theta = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}\,d\theta$.
4. $= \big[\frac\theta2 + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{4}\big]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac\pi4$.

Check: The graph of $y = \sqrt{1-x^2}$ on $[0, 1]$ is the quarter circle in the first quadrant, with area $\frac14\pi\cdot 1^2$.

Tip: Changing the limits to $\theta$ avoids drawing a triangle to convert back.
cards.searchQuery: integral sqrt(1-x^2) 0 to 1 trig substitution quarter circle

cards.title: Why can $\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}$ not be written directly as $\frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+1}$, and what must be done first?
cards.body:
The numerator must have lower degree than the denominator; here the degrees are equal, so divide first: $\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1} = 1 + \frac{2}{x^2-1}$, and only the remainder is decomposed.

The decomposition of the proper part is $\frac{2}{x^2-1} = \frac{1}{x-1} - \frac{1}{x+1}$, so $\int\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}\,dx = x + \log|x-1| - \log|x+1| + C$.

Why: A sum $\frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+1}$ tends to $0$ as $x \to \infty$, but $\frac{x^2+1}{x^2-1}$ tends to $1$. No constants $A$ and $B$ can match that.

Tip: Use polynomial long division whenever $\deg P \ge \deg Q$.

cards.title: How is the **area between curves** $y = f(x)$ and $y = g(x)$ on $[a, b]$ computed when $f(x) \ge g(x)$ throughout?
cards.body:
$\int_a^b \big(f(x) - g(x)\big)\,dx$: integrate the height of the gap, top curve minus bottom curve.

Why: Thin vertical strips have height $f(x) - g(x)$ and width $dx$, and the integral adds up their areas as a limit of Riemann sums.

Example: For $y = x$ and $y = x^2$ the curves meet where $x = x^2$, that is, at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, with $x \ge x^2$ between them. The area is $\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \frac12 - \frac13 = \frac16$.

Tip: Find the intersection points first, since they usually give the limits. If the curves are easier to describe as $x$ in terms of $y$, slice horizontally and integrate in $y$.
cards.searchQuery: area between two curves integral top minus bottom

cards.title: State the **washer method** for the solid made by rotating $\{a \le x \le b,\ g(x) \le y \le f(x)\}$ about the $x$-axis, where $0 \le g \le f$, and its special case the **disk method**.
cards.body:
$V = \pi\displaystyle\int_a^b \big(f(x)^2 - g(x)^2\big)\,dx$; with $g = 0$ this is the disk method, $V = \pi\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx$.

Why: Cutting the solid by a plane perpendicular to the axis gives a ring (a washer) with outer radius $f(x)$ and inner radius $g(x)$, of area $\pi\big(f^2 - g^2\big)$. Then volume is the integral of the slice area, $V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx$.

Example: $y = \sqrt x$ for $0 \le x \le 4$ rotated about the $x$-axis: $V = \pi\int_0^4 x\,dx = 8\pi$.

Watch out: Square each radius first and then subtract. $\pi(f - g)^2$ is wrong.
cards.searchQuery: washer method disk method volume of revolution formula x-axis

cards.title: State the **shell method** for the volume of the solid made by rotating the region under $y = f(x) \ge 0$, $a \le x \le b$ (with $a \ge 0$), about the $y$-axis.
cards.body:
$V = 2\pi\displaystyle\int_a^b x\,f(x)\,dx$

Why: A thin vertical strip at distance $x$ from the axis sweeps out a hollow cylinder. Unrolled, it is a thin slab of length $2\pi x$ (the circumference), height $f(x)$ and thickness $dx$, so its volume is $2\pi x\,f(x)\,dx$.

Example: The region under $y = x$ on $[0, 1]$ about the $y$-axis has $V = 2\pi\int_0^1 x^2\,dx = \frac{2\pi}{3}$. As a check, it is a cylinder of volume $\pi$ with a cone of volume $\frac\pi3$ removed.

Tip: Shells are convenient when the strips run parallel to the axis of rotation, since washers would then require solving for $x$ in terms of $y$.
cards.searchQuery: shell method volume 2 pi x f(x) rotate about y-axis

cards.title: State the **arc length** formula for the graph of $y = f(x)$ on $[a, b]$, where $f'$ is continuous.
cards.body:
$L = \displaystyle\int_a^b \sqrt{1 + \big(f'(x)\big)^2}\,dx$

Why: A tiny piece of the curve is nearly a straight segment with horizontal run $dx$ and vertical rise $dy = f'(x)\,dx$. By Pythagoras its length is $\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2} = \sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx$.

Example: For a line $f(x) = mx$ on $[0, b]$ this gives $b\sqrt{1 + m^2}$, which matches the distance formula.

Watch out: Few choices of $f$ make $1 + f'^2$ a perfect square, so arc length integrals are often hard or must be done numerically.

cards.title: A force of $8\ \mathrm{N}$ holds a spring $0.2\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond its natural length. Assuming Hooke's law, $F(x) = kx$, how much **work** does it take to stretch the spring from its natural length to $0.3\ \mathrm{m}$ beyond it? Give joules.
cards.body:
$1.8\ \mathrm{J}$

Work done by a force $F(x)$ moving an object along a line from $a$ to $b$ is $W = \int_a^b F(x)\,dx$. For a constant force this reduces to force times distance.

1. From $8 = k(0.2)$, $k = 40\ \mathrm{N/m}$.
2. $W = \int_0^{0.3} 40x\,dx = 20x^2\Big|_0^{0.3} = 20(0.09) = 1.8$.
3. Units: newtons times meters is joules.

Watch out: The force grows as the spring stretches, so $F \cdot d$ with the final force would overcount. Hooke's law also holds only for small stretches, not for any extension.
cards.searchQuery: work variable force integral Hooke's law spring joules

cards.title: The region between $y = \sqrt x$ and $y = x^2$ is rotated about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of the solid.
cards.body:
$\frac{3\pi}{10}$

1. The curves meet where $\sqrt x = x^2$, that is, at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$; on $(0, 1)$ we have $\sqrt x > x^2$.
2. The slices are washers with outer radius $\sqrt x$ and inner radius $x^2$.
3. $V = \pi\int_0^1 \big((\sqrt x)^2 - (x^2)^2\big)\,dx = \pi\int_0^1 (x - x^4)\,dx$.
4. $= \pi\big(\frac12 - \frac15\big) = \frac{3\pi}{10}$.

Check: This is smaller than the volume $\frac\pi2$ of the solid made from $y = \sqrt x$ alone, as it should be, since the hole removes some volume.

cards.title: Find the arc length of $y = \frac23 x^{3/2}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 3$.
cards.body:
$\frac{14}{3}$

1. $f'(x) = x^{1/2}$, so $1 + f'(x)^2 = 1 + x$.
2. $L = \int_0^3 \sqrt{1 + x}\,dx$.
3. Substituting $u = 1 + x$ gives $\int_1^4 u^{1/2}\,du = \frac23 u^{3/2}\Big|_1^4$.
4. $= \frac23(8 - 1) = \frac{14}{3}$.

Check: The straight-line distance from $(0, 0)$ to $(3, 2\sqrt3)$ is $\sqrt{9 + 12} \approx 4.58$, and the curve is longer, at $\frac{14}{3} \approx 4.67$.

cards.title: Why is $\int_{-1}^{1}(x - x^3)\,dx = 0$ not the area between $y = x$ and $y = x^3$ on $[-1, 1]$?
cards.body:
The curves cross at $x = 0$, so the top and bottom curves swap there, and the integral gives a net signed area; the true area is $\int_{-1}^{1}|x - x^3|\,dx = \frac12$.

On $[0, 1]$, $x \ge x^3$ and $\int_0^1 (x - x^3)\,dx = \frac12 - \frac14 = \frac14$. On $[-1, 0]$, $x^3 \ge x$ and $\int_{-1}^0 (x^3 - x)\,dx = \frac14$. The two pieces add to $\frac12$.

Why: A region always has positive area, but $\int (f - g)$ counts it negatively wherever $f < g$.

Tip: Find every crossing in the interval, split there, and on each piece subtract bottom from top.

cards.title: Define an **improper integral** over an infinite interval, and over an interval where the integrand is unbounded at an endpoint.
cards.body:
$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t\to\infty}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx$; and if $f$ is continuous on $[a, b)$ but unbounded near $b$, $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = \lim_{t\to b^-}\int_a^t f(x)\,dx$.

If the limit exists and is finite, the integral **converges** to that value; otherwise it diverges. The case of a bad left endpoint is symmetric, with $t \to a^+$.

Example: $\int_1^\infty \frac{dx}{x^2} = \lim_{t\to\infty}\Big(1 - \frac1t\Big) = 1$.

Watch out: If the trouble point is inside $(a, b)$, split the integral there. It converges only if both pieces converge separately.
cards.searchQuery: improper integral definition infinite interval unbounded integrand limit

cards.title: State the **comparison test for integrals** on $[a, \infty)$.
cards.body:
If $f$ and $g$ are continuous with $0 \le f(x) \le g(x)$ for all $x \ge a$, then $\int_a^\infty g$ converging implies $\int_a^\infty f$ converges, and $\int_a^\infty f$ diverging implies $\int_a^\infty g$ diverges.

Why: For $0 \le f \le g$, the integrals $\int_a^t f$ and $\int_a^t g$ both increase with $t$, and the first stays below the second. A growing quantity below a bounded one cannot run off to infinity.

Example: $\int_1^\infty e^{-x^2}\,dx$ converges, because $0 < e^{-x^2} \le e^{-x}$ for $x \ge 1$ and $\int_1^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = e^{-1}$.

Watch out: The inequality must point the right way. Knowing $f \ge g$ with $\int g$ convergent tells nothing about $\int f$.

cards.title: For which real $p$ do the **p-integrals** $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ and $\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx$ converge?
cards.body:
$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p > 1$ (to $\frac{1}{p-1}$); $\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx$ converges exactly when $p < 1$ (to $\frac{1}{1-p}$).

For $p \ne 1$, $\int_1^t x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{t^{1-p} - 1}{1-p}$. As $t \to \infty$ this has a finite limit only if $1 - p < 0$. Likewise $\int_s^1 x^{-p}\,dx = \frac{1 - s^{1-p}}{1-p}$ has a finite limit as $s \to 0^+$ only if $1 - p > 0$.

For $p = 1$ both integrals involve $\log$ and diverge: $\log t \to \infty$ and $-\log s \to \infty$.

Key idea: Each integral is a benchmark for comparison. The two ranges are opposite because a large $p$ helps at infinity and hurts near $0$.

cards.title: State the **trapezoidal rule** $T_n$ for approximating $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$.
cards.body:
$T_n = \dfrac{\Delta x}{2}\Big[f(x_0) + 2f(x_1) + \dots + 2f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\Big]$, with $\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_i = a + i\,\Delta x$.

Why: It adds up the areas of $n$ trapezoids, one over each subinterval, each with area $\frac{\Delta x}{2}\big(f(x_{i-1}) + f(x_i)\big)$. Every interior value appears in two neighboring trapezoids, which is why it has coefficient $2$.

Key idea: $T_n = \frac12(L_n + R_n)$, the average of the left and right sums.

Example: For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 2]$ with $n = 4$, $T_4 = \frac{0.5}{2}\big[0 + 2(0.25 + 1 + 2.25) + 4\big] = 2.75$.
cards.searchQuery: trapezoidal rule formula T_n approximate integral

cards.title: **Simpson's rule** with $n$ even is $S_n = \frac{\Delta x}{3}\big[f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + \dots + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\big]$. Compute $S_4$ and $T_4$ for $\int_0^1\frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx$ (exact value $\pi$) and compare.
cards.body:
$S_4 \approx 3.14157$ and $T_4 \approx 3.13118$; Simpson's error is about $2.4\times 10^{-5}$, the trapezoidal error about $0.0104$.

Simpson's rule replaces the graph on each pair of subintervals by a parabola through three points. Here $\Delta x = 0.25$.

1. Values: $f(0) = 4$, $f(0.25) \approx 3.76471$, $f(0.5) = 3.2$, $f(0.75) = 2.56$, $f(1) = 2$.
2. $S_4 = \frac{0.25}{3}\big[4 + 4(3.76471) + 2(3.2) + 4(2.56) + 2\big] \approx \frac{37.6988}{12} \approx 3.14157$.
3. $T_4 = \frac{0.25}{2}\big[4 + 2(3.76471 + 3.2 + 2.56) + 2\big] \approx 3.13118$.
4. The exact value is $4\arctan 1 = \pi \approx 3.14159$.

Watch out: The weights run $1, 4, 2, 4, \dots, 4, 1$ and need an even number of subintervals.

cards.title: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty x\,e^{-x}\,dx$.
cards.body:
$1$

Write it as $\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_0^t x e^{-x}\,dx$ and use integration by parts.

1. With $u = x$, $dv = e^{-x}\,dx$: $\int x e^{-x}\,dx = -x e^{-x} + \int e^{-x}\,dx = -(x+1)e^{-x}$.
2. $\int_0^t x e^{-x}\,dx = -(t+1)e^{-t} + 1$.
3. $\frac{t+1}{e^t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty$ by L'Hôpital's rule (the form is $\frac\infty\infty$ and the ratio of derivatives is $\frac{1}{e^t}$).
4. So the limit is $1 - 0 = 1$.

Tip: Never plug $\infty$ into an antiderivative as if it were a number. Evaluate the limit explicitly.

cards.title: Give a function for which $\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{-t}^{t} f(x)\,dx$ exists but $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx$ diverges. (By definition, $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f = \int_{-\infty}^{c} f + \int_{c}^{\infty} f$, and both pieces must converge.)
cards.body:
$f(x) = x$

For every $t$, $\int_{-t}^{t} x\,dx = \frac{t^2}{2} - \frac{t^2}{2} = 0$, so the symmetric limit is $0$.

But $\int_0^\infty x\,dx = \lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{t^2}{2} = \infty$, so the half-line pieces diverge and, by the definition, so does $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\,dx$.

Why: The symmetric limit lets the infinite positive and negative areas cancel. The two-sided integral requires each end to be settled on its own, with the two ends going to infinity independently.

cards.title: Why is “doubling $n$ halves the error of the trapezoidal rule” false in general, and what happens for Simpson's rule?
cards.body:
The trapezoidal error bound is proportional to $\frac{1}{n^2}$, so doubling $n$ cuts the error by about a factor of $4$; Simpson's bound is proportional to $\frac{1}{n^4}$, a factor of $16$.

Bounds, for $f$ with continuous derivatives: $|E_T| \le \frac{K(b-a)^3}{12n^2}$ if $|f''| \le K$, and $|E_S| \le \frac{M(b-a)^5}{180n^4}$ if $|f^{(4)}| \le M$.

Example: For $\int_0^1\frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx$ the trapezoidal errors are about $0.01042$, $0.00260$ and $0.00065$ for $n = 4, 8, 16$. Each doubling divides the error by about $4$.

Watch out: These are bounds. A particular function can behave better than the bound, but not worse. For this reason, Simpson's rule is usually far more efficient per function evaluation.

cards.title: Define precisely what it means for a **sequence** $(a_n)$ to be a **convergent sequence** with limit $L$.
cards.body:
For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is an $N$ such that $|a_n - L| < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$; we write $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = L$.

A **sequence** is a function from the positive integers to $\mathbb{R}$, written $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ A sequence that has no such $L$ diverges.

Why: In words, the terms eventually stay inside every window around $L$, however narrow. It is the definition of a limit at infinity, with the variable restricted to integers.

Example: $a_n = \frac1n$ converges to $0$. Given $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $N > \frac1\varepsilon$. Then $n \ge N$ gives $\left|\frac1n - 0\right| = \frac1n \le \frac1N < \varepsilon$.

Watch out: Only the tail matters. Changing finitely many terms never changes whether or to what the sequence converges.
cards.searchQuery: convergent sequence definition epsilon N limit of a sequence

cards.title: Define a **monotone sequence** and a **bounded sequence**.
cards.body:
Monotone: $a_{n+1} \ge a_n$ for all $n$ (increasing), or $a_{n+1} \le a_n$ for all $n$ (decreasing). Bounded: there is a number $M$ with $|a_n| \le M$ for all $n$.

Example: $\frac1n$ is decreasing and bounded. $(-1)^n$ is bounded but not monotone. $n^2$ is monotone but not bounded.

Key idea: Boundedness caps the size of the terms. Monotonicity rules out oscillation. Either alone is not enough for convergence, but both together are, as the next card shows.

Tip: To test monotonicity, compare $a_{n+1}$ with $a_n$ directly (difference or ratio), or differentiate a function $f$ with $f(n) = a_n$ and check the sign of $f'$.
cards.searchQuery: monotone sequence bounded sequence definition increasing decreasing

cards.title: State the **monotone convergence theorem** for sequences.
cards.body:
Every bounded monotone sequence of real numbers converges: an increasing sequence bounded above converges to the smallest number that is at least every term, and a decreasing sequence bounded below converges to the largest number that is at most every term.

Key idea of the proof (increasing case): The terms have a smallest upper bound $L$, since the real line has no gaps. For any $\varepsilon > 0$, $L - \varepsilon$ is not an upper bound, so some $a_N > L - \varepsilon$. Monotonicity keeps every later term in $(L - \varepsilon, L]$.

Example: The sequence $\left(1 + \frac1n\right)^n$ is increasing and bounded above by $3$, so it converges. Its limit is the number $e$.

Watch out: The theorem proves a limit exists. It does not say what it is, so finding the value needs another step.
cards.searchQuery: monotone convergence theorem bounded monotone sequence converges

cards.title: For which real $r$ does the sequence $r^n$ converge, and what is the limit?
cards.body:
It converges exactly for $-1 < r \le 1$: the limit is $0$ if $|r| < 1$ and $1$ if $r = 1$.

For $r > 1$ the terms tend to $\infty$; for $r = -1$ they alternate between $-1$ and $1$; for $r < -1$ they alternate in sign with growing size. All of these diverge.

Why the limit is $0$ for $|r| < 1$: The sequence $|r|^n$ is decreasing and bounded below by $0$, so by the monotone convergence theorem it has a limit $L$. Since $|r|^{n+1} = |r|\cdot|r|^n$, taking limits gives $L = |r|\,L$, so $L = 0$. Hence $|r^n| \to 0$, and so $r^n \to 0$.

Tip: This is the engine behind geometric series, which converge exactly when $|r| < 1$.

cards.title: Evaluate $\lim_{n\to\infty} n^{1/n}$.
cards.body:
$1$

An indeterminate form of type $\infty^0$ is best handled with a logarithm.

1. $\log\big(n^{1/n}\big) = \frac{\log n}{n}$.
2. The function $\frac{\log x}{x}$ has the form $\frac\infty\infty$ as $x \to \infty$, and L'Hôpital's rule gives $\lim \frac{1/x}{1} = 0$. So the sequence $\frac{\log n}{n}$ tends to $0$.
3. Since $n^{1/n} = \exp\!\big(\frac{\log n}{n}\big)$ and $\exp$ is continuous, $n^{1/n} \to e^0 = 1$.

Check: $2^{1/2} \approx 1.41$, $10^{1/10} \approx 1.26$, $100^{1/100} \approx 1.047$. The sequence slowly decreases toward $1$ after $n = 3$.

Watch out: To use L'Hôpital's rule on a sequence, apply it to the function of a real variable $x$ with $f(n) = a_n$.
cards.searchQuery: limit n^(1/n) as n goes to infinity equals 1 logarithm

cards.title: Let $a_1 = \sqrt2$ and $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$. Show that $(a_n)$ converges and find its limit.
cards.body:
The sequence converges to $2$.

The plan: prove it is bounded and monotone, apply the monotone convergence theorem, and then solve for the limit.

1. Bounded: $a_1 < 2$. If $a_n < 2$, then $a_{n+1} < \sqrt{2 + 2} = 2$. By induction $0 < a_n < 2$ for all $n$.
2. Increasing: $a_n < 2$ gives $a_n^2 - a_n - 2 = (a_n - 2)(a_n + 1) < 0$, so $a_n^2 < 2 + a_n$, that is, $a_n < a_{n+1}$.
3. By the monotone convergence theorem, $L = \lim a_n$ exists.
4. Take limits in $a_{n+1} = \sqrt{2 + a_n}$, using continuity of the square root: $L = \sqrt{2 + L}$, so $L^2 = L + 2$.
5. Then $(L-2)(L+1) = 0$. Since $L \ge 0$, $L = 2$.

Watch out: Passing to the limit in step 4 assumes the limit exists. That is why steps 1 to 3 must come first.

cards.title: Why is “every bounded sequence converges” false, and what is the true statement?
cards.body:
A bounded sequence can oscillate forever: $a_n = (-1)^n$ satisfies $|a_n| \le 1$ but diverges. Boundedness alone is not enough; adding monotonicity gives convergence, and the converse holds too: every convergent sequence is bounded.

Why a convergent sequence is bounded: Past some index $N$, all terms lie within $1$ of the limit $L$. The finitely many earlier terms have some largest size, so a single bound works.

Key idea: Convergent $\Rightarrow$ bounded, but not the reverse. Bounded and monotone $\Rightarrow$ convergent.

Watch out: Staying inside a fixed window is not the same as settling down. Convergence needs the terms to stay inside every window around some $L$ eventually.

cards.title: Define when the **series** $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$ converges and what its sum is.
cards.body:
Let $s_N = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_N$ be the $N$-th **partial sum**. The series converges to $S$ if the sequence $(s_N)$ converges to $S$, and then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n = S$; otherwise it diverges.

Why: An infinite sum has no meaning until we say how to add infinitely many terms. This definition adds finitely many at a time and asks where the totals settle.

Example: The geometric series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty a r^n$ with $a \ne 0$ has $s_N = a\frac{1 - r^{N+1}}{1 - r}$. It converges to $\frac{a}{1-r}$ when $|r| < 1$, and diverges when $|r| \ge 1$.

Watch out: Convergence of a series is about the sequence of partial sums, not the sequence of terms $a_n$.
cards.searchQuery: series convergence definition partial sums geometric series sum

cards.title: Define **absolute convergence** and **conditional convergence** of a series $\sum a_n$.
cards.body:
$\sum a_n$ converges absolutely if $\sum |a_n|$ converges; it converges conditionally if $\sum a_n$ converges but $\sum |a_n|$ diverges.

Every absolutely convergent series converges, because the positive and negative parts are each controlled by $\sum |a_n|$.

Example: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n^2}$ converges absolutely, since $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ converges. $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}$ converges (to $\log 2$) but $\sum\frac1n$ diverges, so it converges conditionally.

Why it matters: Absolutely convergent series can be rearranged without changing the sum. Rearranging a conditionally convergent series can change the sum, or make it diverge.
cards.searchQuery: absolute convergence conditional convergence series definition

cards.title: State the **integral test** and its consequence for $\sum \frac{1}{n^p}$.
cards.body:
If $f$ is continuous, positive and decreasing on $[1, \infty)$ and $a_n = f(n)$, then $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$ and $\int_1^\infty f(x)\,dx$ either both converge or both diverge. Hence $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges exactly when $p > 1$.

Why: Because $f$ decreases, $\sum_{n=2}^N a_n \le \int_1^N f \le \sum_{n=1}^{N-1} a_n$. Rectangles of height $a_n$ sit under or over the curve, so the partial sums and the integrals are trapped between each other.

Tip: The $p$-series result is the $p$-integral result from before, translated into series.

Watch out: The test decides convergence only. The integral is not the sum of the series.
cards.searchQuery: integral test series p-series convergence positive decreasing

cards.title: State the **comparison test** and the **limit comparison test** for series with positive terms.
cards.body:
Comparison: if $0 \le a_n \le b_n$ for all large $n$, then $\sum b_n$ converging forces $\sum a_n$ to converge, and $\sum a_n$ diverging forces $\sum b_n$ to diverge. Limit comparison: if $a_n, b_n > 0$ and $\lim\frac{a_n}{b_n} = c$ with $0 < c < \infty$, then $\sum a_n$ and $\sum b_n$ both converge or both diverge.

Why: In the limit comparison test, $a_n \approx c\,b_n$ for large $n$, so the two series behave alike up to a constant factor.

Tip: Use benchmark series: geometric series and $p$-series.

Example: $\sum\frac{1}{n^2 + 1}$ converges by comparison with $\sum\frac1{n^2}$, since $\frac{1}{n^2+1} < \frac1{n^2}$.

Watch out: The inequality must favor the conclusion. $a_n \ge b_n$ with $\sum b_n$ convergent proves nothing.
cards.searchQuery: comparison test limit comparison test series positive terms benchmark

cards.title: State the **ratio test** and the **root test**.
cards.body:
Let $L = \lim\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|$. If $L < 1$ the series $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely, if $L > 1$ (or $L = \infty$) it diverges, and if $L = 1$ the test is inconclusive. The root test is identical with $L = \lim |a_n|^{1/n}$.

Why: If $L < 1$, then eventually $|a_{n+1}| \le r|a_n|$ for some $r < 1$, so the terms are bounded by a geometric series.

Example: For $a_n = \frac{n!}{n^n}$, $\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| = \left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n \to \frac1e < 1$, so $\sum\frac{n!}{n^n}$ converges.

Watch out: $L = 1$ tells nothing. $\sum\frac1n$ and $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ both have $L = 1$, yet one diverges and the other converges.

Tip: Use the ratio test with factorials and exponentials, and the root test when $n$ is in an exponent, as in $\sum\left(\frac{n}{2n+1}\right)^n$ with $L = \frac12$.

cards.title: Find the sum of the **telescoping** series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n(n+1)}$.
cards.body:
$1$

Split each term with partial fractions: $\frac{1}{n(n+1)} = \frac1n - \frac1{n+1}$.

1. Partial sum: $s_N = \Big(1 - \tfrac12\Big) + \Big(\tfrac12 - \tfrac13\Big) + \dots + \Big(\tfrac1N - \tfrac1{N+1}\Big)$.
2. Every middle term cancels, leaving $s_N = 1 - \frac{1}{N+1}$.
3. As $N \to \infty$, $s_N \to 1$.

Key idea: A telescoping series collapses because each term cancels part of its neighbor. Writing out the partial sum is how the sum is found.

Watch out: Always take the limit of $s_N$ after canceling. Canceling terms inside an infinite sum without partial sums can give wrong answers.

cards.title: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{3n+1}{n^3+2}$ converges.
cards.body:
It converges.

For large $n$ the terms behave like $\frac{3n}{n^3} = \frac{3}{n^2}$, so compare with the convergent $p$-series $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ ($p = 2 > 1$).

1. All terms are positive.
2. $\dfrac{a_n}{b_n} = \dfrac{(3n+1)\,n^2}{n^3+2} = \dfrac{3n^3 + n^2}{n^3 + 2} \to 3$.
3. The limit is finite and positive, so by the limit comparison test both series converge or both diverge. Since $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ converges, so does the given series.

Why not direct comparison: $\frac{3n+1}{n^3+2}$ is not obviously smaller than $\frac{1}{n^2}$, since it is about three times larger. A constant factor does not affect convergence, which is exactly what limit comparison captures.
cards.searchQuery: limit comparison test (3n+1)/(n^3+2) series converge p-series

cards.title: Decide whether $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{\sqrt n}$ converges, and if so, whether absolutely or conditionally. Use the **alternating series test**.
cards.body:
It converges conditionally.

The alternating series test: if $b_n > 0$, $b_n$ is decreasing and $b_n \to 0$, then $\sum (-1)^{n+1} b_n$ converges.

1. Here $b_n = \frac{1}{\sqrt n}$ is positive, decreasing, and tends to $0$. So the series converges.
2. Absolute convergence would require $\sum\frac{1}{\sqrt n} = \sum\frac{1}{n^{1/2}}$ to converge. It is a $p$-series with $p = \frac12 \le 1$, so it diverges.
3. The series converges but not absolutely, so the convergence is conditional.

Tip: When the test applies, the error in stopping after $N$ terms is at most the first omitted term $b_{N+1}$.
cards.searchQuery: alternating series test (-1)^(n+1)/sqrt(n) conditionally convergent

cards.title: Give a series whose terms tend to $0$ but which diverges. Show that it diverges.
cards.body:
The harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac1n$.

Group terms in blocks that double in size: $1 + \frac12 + \big(\frac13 + \frac14\big) + \big(\frac15 + \dots + \frac18\big) + \dots$. Each block has $2^{k-1}$ terms, each at least $\frac{1}{2^k}$, so each block sums to at least $\frac12$.

Therefore $s_{2^k} \ge 1 + \frac k2$, which tends to $\infty$, so the partial sums are unbounded and the series diverges.

Why it matters: This is why the divergence test is one-way. If $a_n \not\to 0$, the series $\sum a_n$ diverges. But $a_n \to 0$ alone proves nothing.

Watch out: The terms $\frac1n$ shrink, but they shrink too slowly, so the total area grows like $\log N$.
cards.searchQuery: harmonic series diverges terms tend to zero divergence test

cards.title: Why is “an alternating series whose terms tend to $0$ must converge” false?
cards.body:
The alternating series test also requires the sizes $b_n$ to be decreasing; without that, an alternating series with $b_n \to 0$ can diverge.

Example: Take $\frac11 - \frac1{2^2} + \frac13 - \frac1{4^2} + \frac15 - \dots$, with $+\frac1n$ at odd $n$ and $-\frac1{n^2}$ at even $n$. The signs alternate and the terms tend to $0$. The positive terms alone add up to a divergent series (the odd-indexed terms of the harmonic series, which also diverge), while the negative terms form a convergent series. A divergent part with a convergent part gives divergence.

Why: In a convergent alternating series, positives and negatives must cancel almost exactly. Decreasing $b_n$ guarantees this.

Tip: When checking the alternating series test, verify three things: positive, decreasing, tending to $0$.

cards.title: Define a **power series** centered at $a$.
cards.body:
A series of the form $\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n = c_0 + c_1(x-a) + c_2(x-a)^2 + \dots$, where $a$ is the center and the $c_n$ are fixed numbers (the coefficients).

Why: It is a polynomial of infinite degree. Each choice of $x$ turns it into an ordinary series of numbers, so it defines a function on the set of $x$ where that series converges.

Example: $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$ converges for every $x$, while $\sum_{n=0}^\infty n!\,x^n$ converges only at $x = 0$, since the terms grow too fast for any $x \ne 0$.

Watch out: At $x = a$ every term except $c_0$ vanishes, so a power series always converges at its center.
cards.searchQuery: power series definition center coefficients sum c_n (x-a)^n

cards.title: Define the **radius of convergence** and **interval of convergence** of a power series $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$.
cards.body:
There is a number $R$ with $0 \le R \le \infty$ such that the series converges absolutely for $|x - a| < R$ and diverges for $|x - a| > R$; $R$ is the radius of convergence, and the set of all $x$ where the series converges is the interval of convergence.

The interval of convergence is $(a - R, a + R)$ together with whichever endpoints $a \pm R$ the series converges at.

Tip: If $\lim\left|\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}\right|$ exists, then $R$ is its reciprocal (with $R = \infty$ when the limit is $0$, and $R = 0$ when it is $\infty$). This is the ratio test applied to the terms $c_n(x-a)^n$.

Watch out: The definition says nothing about what happens at $|x - a| = R$. Those two points must be tested one at a time.
cards.searchQuery: radius of convergence interval of convergence definition power series ratio test

cards.title: State the theorem on **term-by-term differentiation** and integration of power series.
cards.body:
If $f(x) = \sum c_n(x-a)^n$ has radius of convergence $R > 0$, then on $(a - R, a + R)$, $f$ is differentiable with $f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty n\,c_n(x-a)^{n-1}$, and $\int f(x)\,dx = C + \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{c_n}{n+1}(x-a)^{n+1}$; both new series have the same radius $R$.

Why it matters: Power series behave like polynomials: differentiate and integrate one term at a time. This produces new series, such as those for $\log(1+x)$ and $\arctan x$, from the geometric series.

Watch out: The radius stays the same, but the behavior at the endpoints can change. Differentiating can lose an endpoint where the original converged, and integrating can gain one.
cards.searchQuery: term by term differentiation integration power series same radius theorem

cards.title: Give the power series for $\frac{1}{1-x}$ and its interval of convergence.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{1-x} = \displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n = 1 + x + x^2 + \dots$ for $|x| < 1$.

Why: It is the geometric series with first term $1$ and ratio $x$, which converges to $\frac{1}{1-x}$ exactly when $|x| < 1$.

Key idea: Substituting turns this one series into many. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives $\frac{1}{1+x} = \sum(-1)^n x^n$, and replacing it by $-x^2$ gives $\frac{1}{1+x^2} = \sum(-1)^n x^{2n}$, each valid when the substituted quantity has size less than $1$.

Example: $\frac{1}{1-x}$ at $x = \frac12$ gives $2 = 1 + \frac12 + \frac14 + \dots$.

cards.title: Use term-by-term integration to find a power series for $\log(1+x)$.
cards.body:
$\log(1+x) = \displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n+1}x^n}{n} = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} - \dots$ for $-1 < x \le 1$.

1. For $|t| < 1$, $\frac{1}{1+t} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n t^n$.
2. Integrate from $0$ to $x$ with $|x| < 1$: $\log(1+x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{n+1}}{n+1}$. The constant is $0$ because $\log 1 = 0$.
3. Reindexing gives the formula above. The radius is still $1$.

Endpoints: At $x = -1$ the series becomes the negative of the harmonic series, so it diverges. At $x = 1$ it is the alternating harmonic series, which converges, and the equality still holds there by a theorem of Abel. So $\log 2 = 1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \dots$

Watch out: The integration gives the series only inside $(-1, 1)$ directly. The endpoint $x = 1$ needs the extra theorem.
cards.searchQuery: power series log(1+x) integrate geometric series interval of convergence

cards.title: Find the radius and interval of convergence of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n\,3^n}$.
cards.body:
$R = 3$ and the interval of convergence is $[-3, 3)$.

1. Ratio test on the terms: $\left|\frac{x^{n+1}}{(n+1)3^{n+1}}\cdot\frac{n\,3^n}{x^n}\right| = \frac{|x|}{3}\cdot\frac{n}{n+1} \to \frac{|x|}{3}$.
2. This is less than $1$ exactly when $|x| < 3$, so $R = 3$.
3. At $x = 3$ the series is $\sum\frac1n$, the harmonic series, which diverges.
4. At $x = -3$ it is $\sum\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$, which converges by the alternating series test.
5. So the interval is $[-3, 3)$: the left endpoint is included and the right is not.

Watch out: The ratio test gives no verdict at $|x| = 3$, since the limit there is $1$. The endpoints need separate tests, and they can behave differently.
cards.searchQuery: radius and interval of convergence sum x^n/(n 3^n) endpoints

cards.title: Find the power series of $\arctan x$ and use it to write $\frac\pi4$ as an infinite series.
cards.body:
$\arctan x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}$ for $|x| \le 1$, and $\frac\pi4 = 1 - \frac13 + \frac15 - \frac17 + \dots$

1. Replace $x$ by $-t^2$ in the geometric series: $\frac{1}{1+t^2} = \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n t^{2n}$ for $|t| < 1$.
2. Integrate from $0$ to $x$: $\arctan x = \sum \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{2n+1}$. The constant is $0$ because $\arctan 0 = 0$.
3. At $x = 1$ the series converges by the alternating series test, and Abel's theorem says its sum equals $\arctan 1 = \frac\pi4$.

Watch out: This series converges very slowly. After $1000$ terms the error in $\pi$ is still about $0.001$. It is a nice formula, not a good algorithm.

cards.title: Why is “the series converges at $x = a \pm R$ if $R$ is its radius of convergence” false, and what is true instead?
cards.body:
At $|x - a| = R$ the series may converge at both endpoints, one, or neither; the radius says nothing there, and each endpoint must be tested separately.

Examples, all with $a = 0$ and $R = 1$:

- $\sum x^n$ converges only on $(-1, 1)$, since the terms do not tend to $0$ at $x = \pm1$.
- $\sum\frac{x^n}{n}$ converges on $[-1, 1)$: harmonic series at $1$ (diverges), alternating harmonic series at $-1$ (converges).
- $\sum\frac{x^n}{n^2}$ converges on $[-1, 1]$, since $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ converges.

Why: The ratio and root tests are inconclusive when their limit is $1$, and at an endpoint that is exactly what happens.

cards.title: Define the **Taylor polynomial** $T_n$ of $f$ at $a$, and the **Maclaurin series**.
cards.body:
$T_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k$, for $f$ with $n$ derivatives at $a$. The Taylor series is the same sum with $n \to \infty$, and the **Maclaurin series** is the Taylor series at $a = 0$.

Why: $T_n$ is the one polynomial of degree at most $n$ whose value and first $n$ derivatives at $a$ equal those of $f$. The factor $\frac{1}{k!}$ cancels the $k!$ that appears when differentiating $(x-a)^k$ a total of $k$ times.

Example: For $f(x) = \log x$ at $a = 1$: $f(1) = 0$, $f'(1) = 1$, $f''(1) = -1$, so $T_2(x) = (x - 1) - \frac{(x-1)^2}{2}$.

Key idea: $T_1$ is the linearization, so Taylor polynomials extend linear approximation to higher degrees.
cards.searchQuery: Taylor polynomial definition Maclaurin series formula f^(k)(a)/k!

cards.title: State **Taylor's theorem** with the **Lagrange remainder**.
cards.body:
If $f$ has $n+1$ derivatives on an open interval containing $a$ and $x$, then $f(x) = T_n(x) + R_n(x)$ where $R_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}$ for some $c$ strictly between $a$ and $x$.

Key idea: For $n = 0$ this is the mean value theorem: $f(x) = f(a) + f'(c)(x - a)$. The general case repeats the mean value argument on a function built from $f$ and its derivatives.

Why it matters: It gives an error bound. If $|f^{(n+1)}| \le M$ between $a$ and $x$, then $|f(x) - T_n(x)| \le \frac{M}{(n+1)!}|x-a|^{n+1}$.

Watch out: The point $c$ exists but is unknown. The theorem is used through a bound on $|f^{(n+1)}|$, never through the value of $c$.
cards.searchQuery: Taylor's theorem Lagrange remainder form error bound f^(n+1)(c)

cards.title: State when a smooth function equals its Taylor series: the criterion in terms of the remainder $R_n$.
cards.body:
If $f$ has derivatives of all orders on an open interval $I$ containing $a$, and $x \in I$, then $f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k$ if and only if $R_n(x) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$.

Why: The partial sums of the Taylor series are exactly the polynomials $T_n$, and $f(x) - T_n(x) = R_n(x)$. The partial sums tend to $f(x)$ exactly when the remainder tends to $0$.

Example: Suppose $|f^{(n)}(t)| \le M$ for all $n$ and all $t$ in $I$. Then $|R_n(x)| \le \frac{M|x-a|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} \to 0$, because factorials beat powers. This works for $e^x$ (on any bounded interval), $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.

Watch out: Convergence of the Taylor series at $x$ is a separate matter from equality with $f(x)$. The remainder must go to $0$ for equality.
cards.searchQuery: Taylor series converges to function remainder tends to zero theorem

cards.title: Give the Maclaurin series of $e^x$, $\sin x$ and $\cos x$.
cards.body:
$e^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$, $\sin x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}$, $\cos x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$, each valid for all real $x$.

Why: Every derivative of $e^x$ is $e^x$, which equals $1$ at $0$. The derivatives of $\sin x$ at $0$ cycle through $0, 1, 0, -1$ (so only odd powers appear, with alternating signs), and those of $\cos x$ through $1, 0, -1, 0$. The remainder tends to $0$ in all three cases.

Mnemonic: $\sin$ is odd and has only odd powers; $\cos$ is even and has only even powers.

Tip: Replacing $x$ by $ix$ in the first series and splitting real and imaginary parts gives Euler's formula $e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x$.
cards.searchQuery: Maclaurin series e^x sin x cos x formulas factorials

cards.title: State the **binomial series** for $(1+x)^k$, with $k$ any real number.
cards.body:
$(1+x)^k = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \binom{k}{n}x^n$ for $|x| < 1$, where $\binom{k}{n} = \frac{k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1)}{n!}$ and $\binom{k}{0} = 1$.

Why: The $n$-th derivative of $(1+x)^k$ at $0$ is $k(k-1)\cdots(k-n+1)$, so the Maclaurin coefficient is $\frac{1}{n!}$ times that. For $k$ a nonnegative integer the coefficients vanish from $n = k+1$ on and this is the ordinary binomial theorem.

Example: With $k = \frac12$: $\sqrt{1+x} = 1 + \frac x2 - \frac{x^2}{8} + \frac{x^3}{16} - \dots$ The coefficient of $x^2$ is $\frac{\frac12\cdot(-\frac12)}{2!} = -\frac18$.

Watch out: The generalized coefficient uses a falling product of $n$ factors starting at $k$, so it works for non-integer $k$.
cards.searchQuery: binomial series (1+x)^k generalized binomial coefficient |x|<1

cards.title: Use Maclaurin series to evaluate $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x - x}{x^3}$.
cards.body:
$-\frac16$

Replace $\sin x$ by its series, $x - \frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{x^5}{120} - \dots$.

1. $\sin x - x = -\frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{x^5}{120} - \dots$
2. Divide by $x^3$: $\frac{\sin x - x}{x^3} = -\frac16 + \frac{x^2}{120} - \dots$
3. Every term after the first has a positive power of $x$, so the limit as $x \to 0$ is $-\frac16$.

Check: L'Hôpital's rule agrees after three rounds: $\frac{\cos x - 1}{3x^2}$, then $\frac{-\sin x}{6x}$, then $\frac{-\cos x}{6} \to -\frac16$.

Tip: Keep just enough terms to see the lowest power of $x$ left after dividing. Series often replace several rounds of L'Hôpital's rule.
cards.searchQuery: limit sin x - x over x^3 Maclaurin series -1/6

cards.title: Let $T_n$ be the degree-$n$ Maclaurin polynomial of $e^x$. Use the Lagrange remainder and $e < 3$ to find the smallest $n$ for which the bound guarantees $|e - T_n(1)| < 0.001$.
cards.body:
$n = 6$

Taylor's theorem at $x = 1$ gives $R_n(1) = \frac{e^c}{(n+1)!}$ for some $c \in (0, 1)$. Since $e^c < e < 3$, $|R_n(1)| < \frac{3}{(n+1)!}$.

1. We need $\frac{3}{(n+1)!} < 0.001$, that is, $(n+1)! > 3000$.
2. $6! = 720$ is too small and $7! = 5040$ works, so $n + 1 = 7$ and $n = 6$.
3. For $n = 5$ the bound is $\frac{3}{720} \approx 0.0042$, which does not guarantee it.

Check: $T_6(1) = \sum_{k=0}^6\frac1{k!} \approx 2.71806$, and $e \approx 2.71828$ differs from it by about $0.00023$.

Watch out: A bound that fails does not prove the approximation is bad. Here, though, $n = 5$ really does fail, since $e - T_5(1) \approx 0.0016$.
cards.searchQuery: Lagrange remainder bound approximate e error less than 0.001 Maclaurin polynomial

cards.title: Let $f(x) = x^2\cos x$. Find $f^{(10)}(0)$.
cards.body:
$90$

The Maclaurin coefficient of $x^{10}$ is $\frac{f^{(10)}(0)}{10!}$. Differentiating ten times by hand is hopeless, but the series gives that coefficient directly.

1. $\cos x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$, so $x^2\cos x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+2}}{(2n)!}$.
2. The power $x^{10}$ needs $2n + 2 = 10$, that is, $n = 4$, with coefficient $\frac{(-1)^4}{8!} = \frac1{8!}$.
3. So $\frac{f^{(10)}(0)}{10!} = \frac{1}{8!}$ and $f^{(10)}(0) = \frac{10!}{8!} = 10\cdot 9 = 90$.

Why this is legitimate: a power series that represents $f$ near $0$ must be the Maclaurin series of $f$, so its coefficients are $\frac{f^{(k)}(0)}{k!}$.

cards.title: Give a function that has derivatives of all orders at $0$ but is not equal to its Maclaurin series on any interval around $0$.
cards.body:
$f(x) = e^{-1/x^2}$ for $x \ne 0$, with $f(0) = 0$.

Every derivative of $f$ at $0$ is $0$. Away from $0$, each derivative has the form (polynomial in $\frac1x$)$\cdot e^{-1/x^2}$, and $e^{-1/x^2}$ tends to $0$ faster than any power of $x$, so each difference quotient at $0$ tends to $0$.

So the Maclaurin series is $0 + 0x + 0x^2 + \dots = 0$, yet $f(x) > 0$ for every $x \ne 0$. The series converges everywhere, but to the wrong function.

Why it matters: The remainder $R_n(x)$ does not tend to $0$ here. Having all derivatives is not enough for a function to equal its Taylor series.

cards.title: Why is “a function that is smooth at every real number has a Taylor series that converges for every real $x$” false?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{1+x^2}$ has derivatives of all orders at every real $x$, but its Maclaurin series $\sum(-1)^n x^{2n}$ converges only for $|x| < 1$.

At $|x| = 1$ the terms are $\pm1$ and do not tend to $0$, and for $|x| > 1$ they grow.

Why: The reason is invisible on the real line. In the complex numbers, $1 + x^2 = 0$ at $x = \pm i$, which are at distance $1$ from the center $0$, and the series cannot reach beyond them.

Watch out: At $x = 1$ the function equals $\frac12$ and is perfectly tame, yet the series there is $1 - 1 + 1 - \dots$, which diverges. The domain of the function says nothing about where its Taylor series converges.
